_comment: Introductions shown in the hero on each book page. Every one names the compiler, when it was put together, and what it was for - that is the minimum a reader needs and the thing most often left out. Keyed by page slug rather than book name: book_blurbs.json derives its key by slugifying the name it carries, which silently lost Al-Tawḥīd and Muʿjam al-Aḥādīth al-Muʿtabara when that name did not match the catalogue's.
al-kafi: Compiled by Muḥammad b. Yaʿqūb al-Kulaynī (d. 329/941) over roughly twenty years in Rayy and Baghdad, during the period of the shorter occultation. His aim was to give a community that had just lost direct access to its Imams a single reliable reference, and he worked close enough to their circles to draw on the companions' own notebooks. It runs in three parts: the Uṣūl on reason, divine unity and the imamate; the Furūʿ on law and practice; and the Rawḍa, a miscellany of sermons and letters. The earliest of the Four Books, the most cited, and the reason much of the earlier written tradition survives at all.
man-la-yahduruh-al-faqih: Written by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) late in his life for a patron in Balkh who had no scholar nearby to consult, and named after a medical handbook made for the same predicament. The second of the Four Books, and the most opinionated: rather than record everything transmitted, al-Ṣadūq included only what he was prepared to rely on, saying he offered these reports as proof between himself and God. It is organised as a working legal reference, from purity and prayer through commerce, marriage and inheritance. Chains are shortened in the text, with the full paths collected in the mashyakha at the end.
nahj-al-balagha: Selected around the turn of the fifth/eleventh century by al-Sharīf al-Raḍī (d. 406/1015), a Baghdadi poet and scholar who gathered the sermons, letters and sayings of Imam ʿAlī he judged most eloquent. That was the project: a literary anthology rather than a complete record, arranged as sermons, then correspondence, then several hundred aphorisms. Its range runs from creation and the limits of describing God to the letter of instruction to Mālik al-Ashtar on governing Egypt, read on its own as a treatise on just rule. Because al-Raḍī chose by literary criterion and often dropped chains, its transmission has been debated as long as it has been read.
al-amali: The 'dictations' of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991), recorded across teaching sessions held in Rayy, Nishapur and Baghdad in the second half of the fourth century, each assembly dated and placed. It is not a compiled reference but a record of teaching: the material moves as a lesson moves, from ethics to the lives of the Prophet and the Imams to a point of doctrine, and several sessions take their subject from the day they fell on, including those on Karbalā. Read straight through it shows what a leading scholar chose to put in front of an audience, and in what order.
al-khisal: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) arranged this one entirely by number: traditions enumerating one thing, then two, then three, ascending through the book. The ordering is a memory device rather than a subject index — it is how material was held before it could be looked up — so a chapter moves from the three things that ruin a person to the three that save him. The effect is to put unrelated material side by side, spanning ethics, law, cosmology and history. It preserves a great deal found nowhere else, including the long treatise on rights attributed to Imam Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn.
kitab-al-ghayba: Shaykh al-Ṭūsī (d. 460/1067) wrote this in Baghdad in the mid fifth/eleventh century, more than a hundred years into the occultation and at a moment when the doctrine was under sustained attack. The purpose is argument as much as collection: he sets out the reports, reasons from them, then answers opponents directly — that a leader nobody can reach is no leader, that the concealment has lasted too long, that the accounts conflict. He documents the four deputies of the shorter occultation and the claimants he rejects, and collects earlier cases of concealment among prophets to argue the pattern is not new.
thawab-al-a-mal-wa-iqab-al-a-mal: Two complementary works of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991), written to be read together and usually printed as one: the rewards promised for particular acts, and the punishments warned of for particular sins. The pairing is the design — the same ground covered from both directions, so a subject can be met as encouragement and as warning. Entries are short and concrete, which is why they are among the most quoted sources in sermons, and also why they draw criticism: several chains are weak, and al-Ṣadūq transmitted more readily in this genre than in law. A map of what the tradition treats as consequential, rather than a legal authority.
uyun-akhbar-al-rida: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) assembled this for the Buyid vizier al-Ṣāḥib b. ʿAbbād, gathering everything he could find on ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā, the eighth Imam. The project was biographical rather than topical, and it is the only book of its kind among his works: sayings and correspondence, the journey to Khurāsān, the appointment as heir apparent by al-Maʾmūn and the politics behind it, the recorded debates at court with Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian scholars, the report known as the Golden Chain, and the circumstances of his death at Ṭūs. It remains the main source for the period it covers.
ma-ani-al-akhbar: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) compiled this to solve a specific problem: reports whose wording is clear and whose sense is not. It collects narrations that explain difficult words, obscure phrases and statements that appear strange on their surface — several of them raised by opponents as objections. The method is what makes it unusual: the explanation is itself a transmitted narration, an Imam asked what something means, so the whole commentary is built from other reports rather than the compiler's own gloss. One of the earliest attempts in the tradition to treat interpretation as a transmitted science rather than individual judgement.
kamil-al-ziyarat: Ibn Qūlawayh (d. 368/978), a Qummi scholar and teacher of al-Shaykh al-Mufīd, wrote the earliest surviving work devoted to ziyāra — the visitation of the Prophet and the Imams, and above all of Imam al-Ḥusayn at Karbalā. Across a hundred-odd chapters it gathers the merit of the visit, its rites and words, the standing of Karbalā's earth, and accounts of those who made the journey when it was dangerous to do so. It is cited nearly as often for its preface, where the author states he included only what reached him through reliable transmitters — a claim scholars have argued over ever since.
al-tawhid: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) wrote this as an argument, not a survey. It gathers narrations on God's oneness, His names and attributes, His knowledge, will and justice, and the refusal to liken Him to anything created — assembled against two positions he regarded as errors: an anthropomorphism that read reports of God's hand or face literally, and a determinism that made human action meaningless and divine justice empty. The arrangement follows that polemic, and several chapters carry recorded debates with dualists, materialists and Muslim opponents in which the case is argued rather than asserted. The standard early Imāmī statement on the subject.
mu-jam-al-ahadith-al-mu-tabara: Compiled by Muḥammad Āṣif Muḥsinī (1935–2019), the Afghan jurist and scholar, and published in the 2000s. The project is stated in the title: to gather only those narrations he judged reliable, working through the standard collections and setting aside what his criteria excluded. That inverts the usual arrangement, in which a collection gathers broadly and leaves assessment to the reader — here the assessment comes first, and the grounds for it are given. Useful for one particular question: which reports on a subject survive a strict standard of transmission. Best read beside the older collections, since what it excludes is as much a claim as what it keeps.
kitab-al-zuhd: Al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī, a companion of the eighth, ninth and tenth Imams writing in the third/ninth century, who later settled in Qum. Its subject is renunciation: detachment from the world, restraint in appetite and speech, the remembrance of death, and the fear and hope the tradition treats as the proper posture toward God. The reports are short, unadorned and grouped by theme. What gives it particular value is its position in the chain — it belongs to the generation of primary written sources that al-Kulaynī, al-Ṣadūq and al-Ṭūsī drew on, so it shows the raw material of the great collections before they absorbed it.
kitab-al-du-afa: A work of rijāl rather than hadith, attributed to Aḥmad b. al-Ḥusayn Ibn al-Ghaḍāʾirī of Baghdad in the fifth/eleventh century. Its purpose is narrow and technical: entries on transmitters judged weak, unreliable or fabricators, consulted when weighing whether a chain can carry the claim placed on it. Two things make it contested. Its judgements are far more severe than comparable works, condemning narrators al-Najāshī and al-Ṭūsī accept. And the attribution itself is doubted, since the book survives through quotation in later works rather than a continuous manuscript. It is therefore rarely used alone — a weakening found only here is weighed against the other rijāl books.
kitab-al-mu-min: Al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī, writing in the third/ninth century as a companion of three Imams, on the believer: their standing before God, the trials they are said to meet, and — the greater part of the book — the rights believers hold over one another. Visiting the sick, meeting a need before being asked, keeping a secret, withholding a harm: concrete, mutual, and stated as obligations rather than virtues, with several reports making the treatment of a believer a direct measure of one's standing with God. Like his Kitāb al-Zuhd it is early and thematic, and passages recur in al-Kāfi in a form close to this one.
sifat-al-shi-a: A short work of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) setting out what the Shīʿa are held to be — the conduct, obligations and character the narrations attach to the name. It reads as a standard rather than a description: how such a person prays, deals in the market, speaks of others and keeps trusts, with several reports stating plainly that the name without the conduct is not the thing, and others distinguishing those who follow the Imams in loyalty alone from those who follow them in practice. Brief and pointed, and ordinarily read alongside Faḍaʾil al-Shīʿa, which takes the other side of the same subject.
risalat-al-huquq: A treatise attributed to Imam ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (d. 95/713), transmitted through Abū Ḥamza al-Thumālī and preserved by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq within al-Khiṣāl. It is unusual in this corpus for being one continuous argument rather than a gathering of separate reports. It enumerates around fifty rights in a single sequence moving outward from the self: the right of God, then of one's tongue, hearing, sight and limbs, then of prayer and fasting, then of those one leads, follows, teaches, learns from, owes and lives beside. Each is stated as an obligation owed rather than a claim held, which is what gives it its force.
fada-il-al-shi-a: A brief collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) on the merits promised to the Shīʿa — forgiveness, intercession, the standing of their dead, and recompense for the hardship that adherence brought in the periods when it was dangerous to profess, which is the setting most of this material comes from. It is the companion piece to Ṣifāt al-Shīʿa: where that book sets out the conduct expected, this one sets out what is promised in return, and the two are ordinarily read and printed together. Its brevity is part of its character — no argument, no commentary, simply the reports on one subject gathered in one place.
